subject: Environment
topic: Climate science II — tipping points — mixed tiers
description: Permafrost, albedo, ocean acidification, feedback loops

questions.stem: 'Permafrost' — ground that remains frozen for two or more consecutive years — is a major climate concern because, on melting, it releases:
questions.explanation: Permafrost (mostly in Siberia, Alaska, northern Canada) locks up ~1.5 trillion tonnes of carbon — twice as much as currently in the atmosphere. As it thaws, microbes decompose the organic matter, releasing CO₂ aerobically and methane (CH₄) anaerobically. Methane is ~25× stronger as a GHG than CO₂ over 100 years. This is a major 'positive feedback' — warming triggers release that causes more warming.

questions.stem: The 'albedo' of a surface measures its:
questions.explanation: Albedo = fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected back to space (0 = pure absorber; 1 = perfect mirror). Fresh snow ~0.80; sea ice ~0.50-0.70; dark ocean ~0.06; forests ~0.10-0.15. When ice melts, darker ocean is exposed — lower albedo — more absorption — more warming. This 'ice-albedo feedback' is why the Arctic warms ~4× faster than the global average.

options.option_text: Absorption of atmospheric CO₂ by seawater

questions.explanation: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid) — seawater has taken up roughly 25-30 % of human CO₂ emissions, lowering surface pH from 8.2 (pre-industrial) to ~8.1 today. Lower pH dissolves the calcium-carbonate shells of corals, pteropods and certain plankton. Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication (oxygen depletion), a different problem. Plastic and oil are physical pollutants.

questions.stem: In the context of the IPCC Assessment Reports, 'RCP 8.5' refers to:
questions.explanation: RCP (Representative Concentration Pathway) 8.5 — named for its radiative forcing of +8.5 W/m² by 2100 — is the highest-emission scenario in IPCC AR5 (2014). The lower pathways — RCP 6.0, 4.5, 2.6 — represent progressively deeper mitigation. AR6 (2021-22) replaced RCPs with the broader Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), combining emission pathways with socio-economic storylines.

questions.stem: Glacial retreat in the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region affects billions of downstream people chiefly through changes in:
questions.explanation: Himalayan and Karakoram glaciers feed the upper Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra — crucial for dry-season (post-monsoon, spring) flows that keep the rivers running when the monsoon is absent. As glaciers retreat, flows initially INCREASE (extra melt), then DECLINE as the ice mass shrinks — 'peak water' is expected mid-century in many basins. ~2 billion people across South Asia depend on these rivers.

options.option_text: A source that emits carbon into the atmosphere
A natural or artificial reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases
A basin where coal is mined
A storage device for fossil fuels

questions.explanation: Carbon sink — a natural or engineered reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it emits — slowing climate change. The three largest natural sinks are oceans (25-30 % of human emissions), land vegetation / soils (~25 %), and the atmosphere (~50 %, the part that stays). 'Blue carbon' sinks are coastal (mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes). India's NDC under Paris includes creating an additional ~2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent sink through forest / tree cover by 2030.

questions.stem: The term 'tipping point' in climate change refers to:

options.option_text: The budget allocated to climate action
A threshold beyond which change becomes self-sustaining
The moment sea level exceeds high-tide mark
The election date of a climate-sceptic government

questions.explanation: A tipping point is a critical threshold where small additional forcing pushes a climate subsystem into a new state that is hard or impossible to reverse. Documented examples — Amazon rainforest die-back, Greenland / West Antarctic ice-sheet collapse, Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation shutdown, boreal forest die-off, coral-reef collapse. IPCC AR6 (2021) raised concern that several tipping points may activate at warming levels as low as 1.5-2 °C.
